title: Property Management 2FA: Go SMS Sender Compliance and Incident Alert Controls
description:
TL;DR: Choose an SMS capability only after it can produce the sender-registration evidence your US and EU launch requires, and keep country allowlists, abuse limits, and cost circuit breakers in your own application. For a property-management platform, the durable design is a small internal OTP contract: the provider behind it can change, while leaseholder login and security-incident alert code does not. Infrai is a reasonable fit when that stable contract and centrally managed origination assets matter, but it is one candidate, not a substitute for regional compliance review.

The uncomfortable trade-off is operational. A direct provider can expose deep, provider-specific controls, while an abstraction can reduce key, SDK, and billing sprawl; neither choice transfers accountability for consent, recipient validity, sender registration, or abuse prevention away from the property manager. I would make the go-live gate evidence-based: no approved origination identity, no traffic.

What should drive 2FA login SMS provider and sender selection?

Consider a bounded pre-production exercise, not a claimed customer incident. A team is preparing login codes for US tenants and EU property staff, plus urgent account-takeover alerts. The happy-path test delivers. The readiness review then asks three less comfortable questions: Which approved sender will originate each country's traffic? Where is the registration decision recorded? What stops an attacker from generating thousands of messages to an expensive destination?

If those answers live in a vendor console screenshot, a developer's memory, and a permissive country_code field, the system is not ready. Delivery is not the invariant. The invariant is that every send is tied to an approved purpose, an eligible destination, a registered origination identity, and durable evidence of the decision.

No evidence, no send.

This changes the provider selection process. Sender creation, registration, lookup, and status are deployment dependencies, not errands to complete after application code ships. The SMS namespace described by Infrai includes sender registration and sender lookup operations, so a team can prepare region-specific origination identities before enabling traffic. Its public discovery surface also exposes capability schemas without a key. Across the wider platform, that surface reports 295 capabilities in 20 modules, including 41 communication routes; those counts describe breadth, not proof that a particular sender is approved. The useful architectural property is that the application's contract stays fixed when the implementation behind that capability moves; the second-order benefit is a single operational credential rather than another provider key distributed through the estate.

There is a catch. Templates and sender assets can require preconfiguration, and an application should retain its own mapping from business purpose and locale to template ID instead of treating a provider catalog as the source of truth. This matters during an audit: tenant_login + de-DE -> template_42 is evidence a reviewer can follow, while "the provider chose something" is not.

Build the compliance record before the send

A useful send ledger is deliberately boring. Store the internal user and property identifiers, purpose (login_otp or security_alert), normalized destination country, consent or other applicable authorization reference, selected sender asset, template revision, provider request ID, and timestamps. Do not put the OTP itself in that record. Set retention and access rules with counsel and the security team; the correct period depends on the legal and contractual context, so a universal number would be fiction.

The decision must happen before network I/O. A provider response can prove that a request was accepted, but it cannot prove that the application was entitled to make it. That boundary belongs in code the platform team owns. After policy approval, the adapter below reads the live discovery contract for the hosted OTP capability. It deliberately does not invent an OTP payload: the schema returned by discovery is the authority the build should validate before a release.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type SendRequest struct {
    UserID          string
    PropertyID      string
    Purpose         string
    Country         string
    SenderAssetID   string
    TemplateID      string
    AuthorizationID string
}

type Policy struct {
    AllowedCountries map[string]bool
    SenderByCountry  map[string]string
    TemplateByKey    map[string]string
}

type Evidence struct {
    UserID, PropertyID, Purpose, Country string
    SenderAssetID, TemplateID            string
    AuthorizationID                     string
    DecidedAt                           time.Time
}

func authorize(req SendRequest, policy Policy, now time.Time) (Evidence, error) {
    if req.Purpose != "login_otp" && req.Purpose != "security_alert" {
        return Evidence{}, errors.New("purpose is not approved")
    }
    if !policy.AllowedCountries[req.Country] {
        return Evidence{}, errors.New("destination country is blocked")
    }
    sender, ok := policy.SenderByCountry[req.Country]
    if !ok || sender != req.SenderAssetID {
        return Evidence{}, errors.New("sender asset is not approved for country")
    }
    key := req.Purpose + ":" + req.Country
    template, ok := policy.TemplateByKey[key]
    if !ok || template != req.TemplateID {
        return Evidence{}, errors.New("template is not approved for purpose and country")
    }
    if req.AuthorizationID == "" {
        return Evidence{}, errors.New("authorization evidence is missing")
    }

    return Evidence{
        UserID: req.UserID, PropertyID: req.PropertyID,
        Purpose: req.Purpose, Country: req.Country,
        SenderAssetID: sender, TemplateID: template,
        AuthorizationID: req.AuthorizationID, DecidedAt: now.UTC(),
    }, nil
}

func loadOTPContract(client *http.Client) ([]byte, error) {
    baseURL := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), "/")
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if baseURL == "" || apiKey == "" {
        return nil, errors.New("INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required")
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, baseURL+"/v1/discovery/sms.otp", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, errors.New("discovery rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func main() {
    policy := Policy{
        AllowedCountries: map[string]bool{"US": true, "DE": true},
        SenderByCountry:  map[string]string{"US": "sender_us_primary", "DE": "sender_de_primary"},
        TemplateByKey:    map[string]string{"login_otp:US": "otp_en_v3", "login_otp:DE": "otp_de_v2"},
    }
    req := SendRequest{
        UserID: "usr_1042", PropertyID: "prop_81", Purpose: "login_otp",
        Country: "DE", SenderAssetID: "sender_de_primary", TemplateID: "otp_de_v2",
        AuthorizationID: "authz_2026_0184",
    }

    evidence, err := authorize(req, policy, time.Now())
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    contract, err := loadOTPContract(&http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second})
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("approved purpose=%s country=%s sender=%s at=%s\n",
        evidence.Purpose, evidence.Country, evidence.SenderAssetID,
        evidence.DecidedAt.Format(time.RFC3339))
    fmt.Printf("loaded OTP contract bytes=%d\n", len(contract))
}

Run the program with INFRAI_BASE_URL set to the API base and INFRAI_API_KEY set through the process secret store. The example stops before delivery on purpose. The verified hosted OTP operation is POST /v1/sms/otp, but its request fields should be taken from the live discovery schema rather than guessed into a sample. A production write adapter must also attach an idempotency key; the platform convention has a 24-hour default deduplication window. That adapter belongs beneath authorize, not mixed into policy evaluation.

Capacity planning starts here too. Set per-user, per-property, per-IP, and per-country limits from the expected login population and alert fan-out, then test the rejection path. The country gate is mandatory because geography-based abuse controls and country-price circuit breakers remain application responsibilities. Small blast radius wins.

Test the refusal path.

Compare control planes, not marketing pages

I would shortlist Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, AWS End User Messaging SMS, and Infrai, then run the same evidence drill against each current contract. Resend belongs in the adjacent email discussion, but not as an equivalent hosted SMS OTP provider. Product names alone settle nothing; registration requirements and capabilities change by destination and sender type, so the decisive artifacts are the current provider documentation and an approved launch record.

Depth beats a long feature list.

Option Architectural fit What to verify before commitment Main trade-off
Twilio Verify Direct verification product Required sender setup, destination coverage, evidence export, and event retrieval A focused product can expose native controls, but application code and operations become tied to its contract
Vonage Verify Direct verification product The same country-by-country sender, template, evidence, and status checks Another direct contract to own; depth should be validated against the exact launch countries
AWS End User Messaging SMS Fits teams already governing messaging through AWS Origination registration, regional availability, IAM boundaries, and audit retrieval Cloud governance may be familiar, while portability follows AWS-specific integration choices
Infrai SMS capability Stable REST capability in front of provider implementations Sender readiness, template mapping, regional behavior, and polling cadence Lower integration churn, with less reason to choose it when deep provider-native controls are the priority
Resend email Email fallback or non-OTP notifications Custom verification logic, suppression handling, and mailbox-provider requirements Email has different delivery and abuse dynamics and is not a like-for-like hosted SMS OTP path

This is a buy-versus-build decision at two layers. Buy carrier connectivity and registration workflow; do not build those. Own the thin policy layer, internal template registry, evidence ledger, and provider-neutral interface because those encode property-management obligations and keep a migration bounded. Buying a managed verification product can reduce auth implementation work, but no provider knows that a particular property employee should receive a security alert at 03:00 while a former contractor should not.

The SLO should measure the user outcome and expose the dependencies: for example, define an internal target for eligible login challenges completed within the application's allowed verification window, then separately track policy rejections, provider acceptance, and verification completion. Do not publish a target copied from a vendor page. Derive it from the login risk model, delivery data, and support tolerance, with an error budget that can actually trigger a country or sender rollback.

Polling changes the incident design

Neither the SMS nor email namespace provides webhook event delivery; status and events are pulled. That means a security-incident workflow cannot assume an immediate delivery callback. Poll with bounded exponential backoff, persist the last observed state, and stop at a deadline tied to the incident's urgency. The polling workers need a capacity estimate based on peak sends multiplied by polls per send, plus jitter so a burst of tenant logins does not become a synchronized status storm.

This is the point at which I would reject a neat-looking multichannel diagram. Email can be a useful fallback, but the email capability has no hosted OTP operation, so an email login-code fallback requires custom authentication logic. There is no SMTP relay, and voice, WhatsApp, and RCS are outside this capability set. A design that labels all of them "fallback" without separate threat models and delivery contracts is unfinished.

Email is different.

Bounces and invalid recipients also belong to the lifecycle, not a cleanup job. For email notifications, check suppression state before sending, add addresses that have become invalid to the suppression process, and reconcile pulled events into the internal recipient record. Yahoo's sender requirements are a useful reminder that mailbox-provider rules apply independently of an API accepting a request. For SMS, maintain the same deny-before-send posture using the available suppression capability and status polling. The ledger should explain why a recipient was excluded without preserving message secrets.

Where this recommendation stops

Use the stable-contract approach when several services need messaging, the platform team wants one integration boundary, and switching the implementation without rewriting callers is valuable. Infrai supports that case through a plain REST surface, one credential, public capability discovery, and per-capability readiness data. Mentioning it once in an architecture review is warranted. Treating it as compliance certification is not.

Choose a direct provider instead when a required country, sender type, registration workflow, or provider-native control is better served there and the lock-in cost is acceptable. Delay launch when counsel or the provider cannot confirm the origination path. For domestic China email compliance, a pending Tencent email vendor is not evidence of readiness. For teams that require push webhooks, SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS, this capability set does not meet the requirement.

My final gate would therefore contain four signed items: approved countries and purposes, registered sender assets, versioned template mappings, and tested application abuse controls. Then I would require a load test of polling capacity and a recovery exercise that swaps the adapter while leaving the caller contract intact. The provider decision follows from that evidence. The logo does not.

Sources

  • Resend documentation: https://resend.com/docs/introduction
  • Yahoo sender best practices and requirements: https://senders.yahooinc.com/best-practices/

title: Migration & Modernization
description:
Migrated an App and PostgreSQL Database from Azure to AWS—And the “Successful” Database Migration Still Needed Fixing

An end-to-end migration lab: private networking, Site-to-Site VPN, AWS DMS full load + CDC, database cutover, and a private EC2 application behind an HTTPS load balancer.

Migration is easy in architecture diagrams. Draw an arrow from Azure to AWS, add a cloud icon, and everyone goes home happy. Real migrations involve routes, ports, replication state, application secrets, database defaults, and at least one moment when an ALB says 504 Gateway Timeout instead of saying hello.

This was a hands-on lab, not a claim about a production enterprise cutover. I built an Azure environment to simulate an on-premises source and migrated a Node.js application and PostgreSQL database to AWS. The goal was to practice the decisions, checks, and failure modes that matter in a real migration.

The part the architecture diagram does not show: Airtel, MTN, and a VPN reality check

My first idea was closer to a traditional on-premises lab: run an Ubuntu VM locally in VirtualBox, connect it to AWS, and migrate the application and database across that private link. The application was the easy part to picture. Getting a reliable, publicly reachable VPN endpoint on the home/mobile-internet side was not.

I explored the connectivity constraints of working through Airtel and MTN connections. A VM behind a laptop, a router, and a mobile provider is often several network translations away from the internet. With carrier-grade NAT (CGNAT), the public address seen by websites may not be an address I can actually terminate an inbound IPsec tunnel on. Port forwarding on my own router would not necessarily solve a translation layer controlled by the provider.

In other words, I wanted to practise an enterprise migration, but first I had to negotiate with the internet connection. The cloud architecture was ready for a Site-to-Site VPN; my mobile-network setup had other ideas.

Rather than pretend the local connection was a reliable on-premises VPN endpoint, I changed the lab design. I deployed a private Ubuntu VM in Azure to simulate the source data centre and used an Azure VPN Gateway with a public endpoint to connect to AWS Site-to-Site VPN. That gave me a repeatable, cloud-to-cloud IPsec path while keeping the source workload private.

This was an architectural compromise, not a claim that Azure is physically on-premises. The important skills were still the same: non-overlapping CIDRs, customer and virtual private gateways, tunnel parameters, routing in both directions, security rules, and proving that real application/database traffic could cross the connection.

The first lesson arrived before DMS even started: if the network cannot provide a usable VPN endpoint, change the lab design—not the definition of success.

What I built

Source (Azure, simulating on-prem): an Ubuntu VM with a private address, a Node.js/Express order-management app on port 3000, and PostgreSQL 16 containing customers, products, and orders.

Target (AWS): a VPC (10.16.0.0/16), private Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, AWS DMS, and a private EC2 instance running the application. An internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB) terminates HTTPS and forwards traffic to the private app on port 3000.

Migration connectivity: a route-based IPsec Site-to-Site VPN between Azure (172.16.0.0/16) and AWS (10.16.0.0/16). The Azure VPN connection showed Connected; on AWS, one VPN tunnel was UP and the other DOWN. That was sufficient for the lab, but not a highly available production VPN design.

                 Migration path (private traffic)
  Azure simulated on-prem                    AWS
  172.16.0.0/16                              10.16.0.0/16
  +----------------------+   IPsec VPN   +----------------------+
  | Ubuntu VM 172.16.0.4|===============>| DMS replication      |
  | Node.js :3000       |                | RDS PostgreSQL       |
  | PostgreSQL 16       |                | Private subnets      |
  +----------------------+                +----------------------+

                 Final application request path
  Browser --HTTPS :443--> Public ALB --HTTP :3000--> Private EC2
                                                   |
                                                   +--TCP :5432--> Private RDS

Security note: This diagram shows the logical data flow, not every route table, gateway, or security-group rule. The public ALB is the entry point; the EC2 application and RDS database do not need public IPs.

Phase 1 — Establish the source environment

I created the Azure virtual network, private workload subnet, VPN gateway subnet, and an Ubuntu VM without a public NIC address. The source VM hosted the application and PostgreSQL database. A private VM is a good simulation of an on-prem server: reaching it requires an intentional management or network path, rather than a casual SSH connection from the internet.

The first screenshot captures the starting point: an Ubuntu VM named on-prem-workload, using private IP 172.16.0.4 without a public NIC address. This was the host running both the Node.js app and the PostgreSQL source database.


Figure 1: The Azure VM used as the simulated on-premises source.

The VM needed more than an IP address: its subnet determined where the workload lived, while Azure reserved a separate GatewaySubnet for the VPN gateway. My VNet was 172.16.0.0/16, with the workload subnet 172.16.0.0/24 and GatewaySubnet 172.16.255.0/24. Keeping those roles separate made it easier to reason about which traffic was local and which had to cross the VPN.


Figure 2: Azure network segmentation for the workload and VPN gateway.

The source database contained three tables: customers, products, and orders. The application exposed a health endpoint and supported reading and writing data, giving me something meaningful to validate after migration.

Phase 2 — Connect Azure to AWS over IPsec

The Azure VPN gateway and AWS virtual private gateway were configured with compatible tunnel parameters. I created an Azure Local Network Gateway representing the AWS VPN endpoint and remote address space. On the AWS side, the private route tables needed a route back to 172.16.0.0/16 through the virtual private gateway.

On the Azure side, I provisioned the route-based Virtual Network Gateway (onprem-vpn-gateway). Its public endpoint was 4.255.22.3. This gateway terminates the encrypted tunnel on Azure’s side; it does not replace the workload VM or act as the application server.


Figure 3: Azure VPN gateway used for the lab connection.

After defining the AWS tunnel endpoint in an Azure Local Network Gateway and creating the IPsec connection, I checked the connection resource. The Connected status shown below told me the VPN negotiation succeeded. It did not, on its own, verify that PostgreSQL traffic could pass through both networks.


Figure 4: The Azure-to-AWS VPN connection in the Connected state.

The AWS side: gateways, routes, and tunnel health

I started by creating the AWS Customer Gateway (CGW), which represents the Azure VPN device. Its peer address was the Azure VPN Gateway's public IP, 4.255.22.3. I then created a Virtual Private Gateway (VGW) and attached it to the AWS VPC (10.16.0.0/16). The CGW represents the remote side; the VGW is the AWS-side termination point. These are different objects, and neither is a subnet route table.

The AWS Customer Gateway configuration identified the Azure VPN Gateway as the remote peer. This was an important detail: the Customer Gateway's IP is not the private IP of my Azure Ubuntu VM.


Figure 5: The AWS Customer Gateway representing the Azure VPN Gateway at 4.255.22.3.

After attaching the VGW to the VPC, I created the AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection using the CGW and VGW with static routing. This resource ties the two gateways together and exposes the AWS tunnel endpoint configuration needed on Azure. For the working tunnel, the AWS outside IP used by Azure was 3.227.45.240. I kept the pre-shared key out of this article.


Figure 6: The AWS VPN connection linking the Customer Gateway and Virtual Private Gateway.

The VPN connection's static route was the first routing layer. I configured 172.16.0.0/16 as the remote Azure address space reachable through this VPN. That tells the static-routing VPN which network sits behind its peer; it does not automatically prove that the VPC subnets will send packets to the VGW.


Figure 7: The VPN-level static route for Azure's 172.16.0.0/16 network.

The VPC subnet route table was the second routing layer. In the AWS private route table, I needed a destination of 172.16.0.0/16 pointing to the VGW. This is the route that lets resources in the relevant AWS subnets send traffic toward the Azure network. The local 10.16.0.0/16 route remains for traffic inside the AWS VPC. Azure also needed a return route for 10.16.0.0/16, plus NSG and host firewall rules allowing the relevant traffic.


Figure 8: AWS VPC private route table, including 172.16.0.0/16 → VGW. This is distinct from the VPN connection's static route in Figure 7.

With both routing layers in place, I checked tunnel state. AWS provides two tunnels, but only Tunnel 1 was UP in this lab; Tunnel 2 remained DOWN. The working tunnel supported the migration, but it was not a highly available production VPN. A tunnel being UP also doesn't prove that TCP 5432 reaches PostgreSQL: routing, source/target security rules, and the database listener still have to be checked.


Figure 9: AWS tunnel status showing one operational tunnel and one unavailable tunnel.

The remaining AWS screenshot documents the private EC2 instance and its security-group context, not a gateway. It is more relevant later, when discussing how the application server was protected behind the ALB, so I have placed it in the application section instead of mislabeling it as a Customer Gateway.

The networking lesson was that CGW + VGW + VPN + tunnel status + VPN static route + VPC subnet route + return route each solve a different problem. A green tunnel indicator alone is not the finish line.

Phase 3 — Prepare AWS RDS and DMS

I provisioned private Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL and set up AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) endpoints for the Azure source database and the AWS target. The source was PostgreSQL 16 and the RDS target reported PostgreSQL 18.3, so this exercise also required attention to engine-version differences and schema compatibility.

Source endpoint: AWS DMS needed a connection definition for PostgreSQL on the Azure VM (172.16.0.4). This endpoint identifies the database DMS reads from; it does not itself copy data. The VPN, database listener, PostgreSQL authentication, and inbound TCP 5432 access all had to work before DMS could read source rows.


Figure 10: AWS DMS source endpoint for the Azure-hosted PostgreSQL database.

Target endpoint: The other endpoint pointed to the private RDS PostgreSQL instance. DMS writes migrated records there, so the RDS security group needed to allow the replication path on TCP 5432. The target was not publicly exposed just to make migration easier.


Figure 11: AWS DMS target endpoint for Amazon RDS PostgreSQL.

I selected full load plus change data capture (CDC). These are two separate phases. Full load copied the rows that already existed in customers, products, and orders to RDS. CDC then tracked subsequent changes from the PostgreSQL source and applied them to the target while the source remained the system of record. The point was to avoid relying on a single database snapshot while new orders or customers might still be added.

I used actual inserts as a functional check of the replication process: records created on the source during the CDC window should appear on the target after DMS catches up. This is different from the post-cutover inserts, which were written directly to RDS after the application was repointed. I would not call CDC verified simply because a task said Running; I needed to observe the resulting rows on both sides. The screenshots show the task and final validation, but they are not a timestamped audit trail of each individual CDC insert.

The migration plan was:

  1. Establish and test private connectivity and database access.
  2. Create and test DMS source and target endpoints.
  3. Run the pre-migration assessment and review warnings.
  4. Run full load and CDC, monitoring task and table status.
  5. Compare data and validate application read/write behavior.
  6. Freeze source writes, confirm target consistency, and stop replication.
  7. Reconfigure and move the application to AWS, then verify end-to-end access.

Phase 4 — Assess, replicate, validate

Once both endpoint connections were configured, I created the azure-postgres-to-rds replication task. This task is the component that performs full load plus CDC; the endpoint objects merely tell it where to connect. The task view was my starting point for tracking its execution rather than assuming the database was ready after the first successful connection test.


Figure 12: The DMS task configured for the migration.

Before trusting the copy, I reviewed the DMS pre-migration assessment. It reported 43 checks: 26 passed, 2 warnings, 15 skipped, and 0 failed. I treated the warnings and skipped checks as prompts for manual review, particularly because replication tools do not guarantee that every schema object will behave identically after cutover.


Figure 13: Pre-migration assessment results.

A useful lesson from this assessment was that zero failed checks does not mean zero migration risks. I still needed to review skipped items and test schema behavior myself.

Next I checked DMS table validation, which compares replicated source and target data for the tables in scope. The validation view showed all three selected tables validated with zero reported mismatches and zero validation errors. This was evidence about replicated table data, not proof that application inserts, sequences, and constraints would all work.


Figure 14: DMS table validation showed three validated tables, with no reported mismatches or validation errors.

I also queried both databases directly rather than relying only on the DMS dashboard. At the comparison point shown here, each side contained 4 customers, 3 products, and 3 orders. Those matching counts provided a simple cross-check, although equal counts alone cannot prove every value or relationship matches.


Figure 15: Comparing source and target row counts during migration.

Together, the table validation and SQL count comparison increased my confidence in the migrated rows. Neither test removed the need to check schema defaults, constraints, and real application transactions.

The gotcha: rows migrated, but the schema was not application-ready

The most useful lesson in this lab was that a healthy-looking DMS task is not the same as a fully functional database cutover.

After replication, I had to repair PostgreSQL schema behavior on the target: sequence-backed IDs, defaults, and missing unique/foreign-key constraints. I also had to grant the application user the required sequence permissions. For example, in a controlled lab where that level of access is appropriate:

GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA public TO appuser;

The precise schema changes depend on the source DDL and migration configuration; the command above is not a universal production permission recipe. In a real migration, I would migrate schema objects explicitly, compare source and target DDL, validate constraints and sequences, and test inserts and updates before approving cutover.

Why it matters: a row-count dashboard can be green while the first real customer insert fails. Databases do not give bonus points for beautiful dashboards.

Phase 5 — Cut over PostgreSQL, including the application DB_HOST

This was the point where the migration stopped being a database-copy exercise and became an application cutover. Copying rows into RDS did not automatically make the Node.js app use RDS: the app still read its database destination from .env.

The sequence I followed was to validate the replicated data, stop writes against the Azure source, make sure the final source changes had reached RDS, and then change the application's database connection to the RDS endpoint. In the lab I changed the source application's .env database host to RDS before moving the application process to AWS. That allowed me to separate the database cutover from the later EC2 rehost.

A simplified example of the key configuration change is:

# Before: PostgreSQL running on the Azure source VM
DB_HOST=172.16.0.4
DB_PORT=5432
DB_NAME=migrationdb

# After: private RDS PostgreSQL endpoint (replace with your own)
DB_HOST=<your-rds-endpoint>.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com
DB_PORT=5432
DB_NAME=migrationdb

I kept the credentials outside the article. Editing .env by itself does not reconfigure an already-running Node.js process: the application must be restarted so it loads the new environment. I then checked that the application could connect to RDS and that reads and writes worked. Because the app was still on Azure at this intermediate stage, the Azure-to-AWS VPN route and the RDS security-group allowance for the Azure source CIDR were necessary for its database traffic.

This exposed a less obvious migration problem. DMS had moved the rows, but the target schema was not yet fully ready for new inserts. PostgreSQL sequence-backed IDs, column defaults, unique/foreign-key constraints, and sequence permissions needed attention on RDS. I repaired those issues and granted the lab application user the necessary sequence access:

GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA public TO appuser;

For sequence-backed IDs, the sequence also needs to be aligned with the already-migrated maximum ID before new writes begin; otherwise, a fresh insert can collide with an existing primary key. That check must be performed for each applicable table using its actual sequence name. These schema repairs were an important reminder that DMS row validation is not schema validation.

Once the app could write to RDS, I inserted additional customer data on the target side. Those new rows confirmed that RDS had become writable for the application; they were not proof of source-to-target CDC, because the writes were no longer originating from Azure PostgreSQL. The original comparison screenshot showed 4 customers, 3 products, and 3 orders on each side at an earlier checkpoint. Later RDS counts were expected to increase after target-only inserts, including an application insert that brought the customer count to six. That difference is intentional, not evidence of replication drift.

After the source-write freeze, consistency checks, and cutover, I stopped the DMS task. A Stopped replication task is expected after a completed one-way migration; it is not a failure if the source of truth has intentionally moved to RDS.


Figure 16: The DMS task stopped deliberately after the database cutover and target-side verification.

Phase 6 — Application cutover: copy the Node.js app from Azure to AWS over SSH

The database migration was only half the job. At this point, the Azure-hosted application had already been repointed to RDS through its .env file, but the application process itself was still running on the Azure VM. My next task was to rehost that workload on AWS without exposing the private EC2 instance to the public internet.

I provisioned an Ubuntu EC2 instance in the AWS private subnet at 10.16.2.80. Because Azure and AWS were already connected by the Site-to-Site VPN, I could transfer the application directly from the Azure VM to the private EC2 address using SSH and SCP. The VPN carried the traffic; neither workload needed a public IP for this transfer.

First, establish SSH access across the VPN

I prepared SSH public-key authentication on the destination EC2 instance by adding the appropriate public key to the destination user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. I also checked that the EC2 security group allowed TCP 22 from the Azure VM/private source address for the migration window, rather than opening SSH to the entire internet. The AWS subnet route back to 172.16.0.0/16 and Azure's route to 10.16.0.0/16 were necessary for the return traffic.

From the Azure source VM, the connectivity check looked like this (example user/key names):

ssh -i ~/.ssh/migration-key ubuntu@10.16.2.80

If SSH failed, I needed to check routing, the VPN tunnel, SSH key permissions, the destination security group, and the instance's SSH service—not immediately assume the application was broken.

Package the application without copying credentials

I packaged the Node.js project on Azure, excluding node_modules and .env. The former should be reinstalled for the target runtime; the latter contains environment-specific settings and potentially credentials that should not be carried across blindly.

# Run on the Azure VM; adjust the project path to your own deployment
cd /path/to/order-management-app

tar --exclude='./node_modules' --exclude='./.env' \
    --exclude='./.git' -czf /tmp/order-management-app.tar.gz .

I then copied the archive over the private VPN path to AWS:

# Run on the Azure VM
scp -i ~/.ssh/migration-key \
  /tmp/order-management-app.tar.gz \
  ubuntu@10.16.2.80:/tmp/

These are reproducible command examples, not a claim that these exact file paths or SSH key names were used in the lab.

Rebuild the runtime on the AWS EC2 instance

After logging into the private EC2 instance, I extracted the archive, installed the Node.js dependencies, and created a fresh .env pointing to the RDS PostgreSQL endpoint, not the old Azure database.

# Run on the AWS EC2 instance
mkdir -p ~/order-management-app
cd ~/order-management-app

tar -xzf /tmp/order-management-app.tar.gz
npm ci  # requires an existing package-lock.json

The target was configured for Node.js 22. The important .env values were:

DB_HOST=<your-private-rds-endpoint>.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com
DB_PORT=5432
DB_NAME=migrationdb
DB_USER=appuser
DB_PASSWORD=<set-securely-on-the-server>
PORT=3000

This was the second environment-configuration step: I had already switched the Azure application's DB_HOST to RDS during the database cutover, and now I configured the new AWS application instance to use that same target database. Simply copying the code would not have changed the database connection automatically.

Run it as a service and verify actual database connectivity

I configured the app as a systemd service called migration-webapp.service so it would run independently of my SSH session and could be restarted and inspected through normal Linux service management.

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now migration-webapp.service
sudo systemctl status migration-webapp.service
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/health

The /health endpoint performed a database connectivity check (SELECT 1), so a healthy response meant more than “the Node.js process is listening.” I also tested application reads and new customer inserts against RDS. Those inserts were post-cutover target-side writes, distinct from the earlier Azure-side inserts used to demonstrate DMS CDC.

The screenshot below belongs here: it shows the AWS private application instance and security-group context. It does not show an AWS Customer Gateway. The final security posture was to allow application TCP 3000 from the ALB security group and PostgreSQL TCP 5432 from the EC2 application security group to RDS. Migration-only SSH access could then be restricted or removed.


Figure 17: Private EC2 destination and its security-group context during the application rehost.

Migration transfer: Azure VM 172.16.0.4 --SSH/SCP over VPN--> AWS EC2 10.16.2.80
Final app path:    Browser --HTTPS 443--> ALB --HTTP 3000--> EC2 --TCP 5432--> RDS

I used SSL for the RDS connection, but the lab's rejectUnauthorized: false setting skipped certificate verification. In production, I would validate the RDS CA certificate, store secrets in a managed secret store, and automate deployments rather than manually SCP an archive.

Phase 7 — Route user traffic through the Application Load Balancer

At this stage, the database was already on RDS, and I had copied the Node.js application from Azure to the private AWS EC2 instance (10.16.2.80). I could reach the application locally on port 3000, but that did not mean an internet user could reach it: the EC2 instance had no public IP, and exposing port 3000 directly would defeat the purpose of keeping the application server private.

I therefore introduced an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB), named testing2, in public subnets. This became the public entry point while the Node.js process continued running privately on EC2. I created the target group testing, selected an instance target, registered the EC2 instance, and configured the target group's protocol as HTTP with port 3000. I set its health-check path to /health, which the application uses to check database connectivity with SELECT 1.

This distinction matters: the ALB listener port is not the application's port. Users connect to the ALB on 443; the listener's forward action selects the target group; and the target group connects to the registered EC2 instance on 3000. Users do not need to know the EC2 private IP or type :3000 in their browser.

I configured two listeners:

  • HTTP 80 → redirect to HTTPS 443. Requests arriving over plain HTTP are redirected to the encrypted endpoint.
  • HTTPS 443 → forward to target group testing (HTTP 3000). An AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate handles TLS termination at the ALB. The application still receives HTTP on the private network, on its own listening port. 
Internet user / browser
        |
        | HTTPS :443
        v
Internet-facing ALB: testing2
        | HTTPS listener :443, TLS termination
        | Forward action -> target group "testing"
        v
Target group: HTTP :3000; health check GET /health
        |
        | Private VPC traffic on TCP :3000
        v
EC2: 10.16.2.80 (Node.js application, port 3000)
        |
        | PostgreSQL connection TCP :5432
        v
Private Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL

The security-group rule that caused a 504

The first ALB test returned 504 Gateway Timeout. The listener existed and the target group was configured, but the ALB could not get a timely response from the application instance. The missing piece was the EC2 security-group ingress rule: it needed to allow TCP 3000 with the ALB security group as the source. I added that rule instead of opening port 3000 to the whole internet. The ALB security group also needed inbound 443 from intended clients, and the EC2 instance needed outbound connectivity to RDS on 5432 with a corresponding RDS inbound rule.

After correcting the rule, I checked that the registered target was Healthy using the /health check, then tested the application through the ALB rather than only using curl localhost:3000 on EC2. A successful local curl proves the process works on the server; a healthy target and successful ALB request prove the load-balancer-to-instance path works as well.

The lab used the ALB DNS name testing2-695509388.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com for connectivity testing. The ACM wildcard certificate *.holadmex.online is valid only for matching custom hostnames, not the AWS-generated elb.amazonaws.com hostname. A production-quality HTTPS user journey would additionally require a matching DNS record and certificate validation. I did not document a completed custom-domain DNS cutover, so I am not claiming one.

Finally, I opened the order-management application through the load-balancer path and tested database-backed reads and new customer inserts. The successful insert was important: the browser was now reaching the AWS-hosted application, and that application was writing to RDS, not back to the old Azure PostgreSQL source. These post-cutover writes are different from the earlier source-side inserts replicated by DMS CDC.


Figure 18: The order-management UI used for end-to-end testing. The screenshot shows the application interface; the ALB target-health, service, and database checks were needed to verify the full request path. Any hard-coded environment label in the UI is not proof of which infrastructure served it.

The end state: Azure PostgreSQL had been replicated and cut over to RDS; the Node.js application had been transferred from the Azure VM to private EC2 using SSH/SCP over the VPN; its new .env pointed DB_HOST to RDS; and users accessed the app through the public ALB, which forwarded traffic to the private instance on port 3000.

What I would check before calling a real production migration complete

  • Network: VPN tunnel redundancy, both-direction routes, SG/NSG policy, DNS resolution, and private-only database access.
  • Database: DDL parity, indexes, constraints, sequences, roles, permissions, row counts, validation errors, application transactions, and a tested recovery path.
  • Cutover: approved freeze window, final CDC lag checks, explicit source-of-truth decision, rollback criteria, and stakeholder sign-off.
  • Application: process supervision, health checks, logs, connection pool settings, TLS validation, secrets management, and ALB target health.
  • Operations: monitoring, backup/restore exercises, runbooks, cost controls, and post-cutover support.

Future modernization (not implemented in this lab)

After a successful rehost, the next stage could be containerizing the app, pushing images to Amazon ECR, deploying to ECS/Fargate or EKS, managing infrastructure with Terraform, using AWS Secrets Manager, adding CI/CD, and strengthening observability. I'd also revisit RDS high availability and VPN redundancy.

Those are next steps, not things I am claiming to have delivered in this migration.

Final thoughts

The biggest takeaway wasn't a service name. It was learning that connectivity, replication, schema fidelity, application behavior, and cutover are five different things—and every one must be validated independently.

A green DMS status is good news. A working application that can read and write safely after cutover is better news. And after the Airtel/MTN connectivity detour, a VPN tunnel carrying actual traffic felt like a milestone of its own.

If you've migrated a database using DMS, what was the trickiest post-migration issue you encountered?

title: Go 1.27 HTTP Router with Generic Methods and Zero-Alloc Routing: FURSY — What an Independent Audit Found at 94% Coverage
description:
We shipped FURSY v0.5.4 thinking it was production-ready. Ninety-four percent test coverage. Thirty-five findings from our internal audit, all fixed. Twelve CI checks across three operating systems. Zero-alloc routing under 100 ns/op.

Then we handed the codebase to an independent auditor. They found the CORS middleware echoing back unfiltered headers to browsers. The SECURITY.md teaching six APIs that don't exist. Error responses claiming RFC 9457 compliance while returning text/plain. A path parser that panics on Google's most widely used REST convention.

This is the story of what went wrong, how we fixed it, and what fursy actually is after the cleanup.

What Is Fursy

FURSY (Fast Universal Routing SYstem) is an HTTP router for Go 1.27+ with three properties that don't usually come together:

  1. Generic methods on the router -- router.POST("/users", handler) where handler receives a typed *Box[CreateReq, UserRes]. Go 1.27 enabled this; to our knowledge, FURSY is the first Go router to ship generic methods on the router type.

  2. Zero-allocation routing -- sub-100 ns/op for static routes, 0 B/op, 0 allocs/op. The radix tree reuses a caller-provided param buffer from sync.Pool.

  3. RFC 9457 Problem Details as the default -- every auto-generated error (404, 405, 401, 429, 500) returns application/problem+json. Not opt-in. Not "if you use our error type." Every response.

We built it as the successor to ozzo-routing, Qiang Xue's router from the Yii framework ecosystem. When Xue handed over the go-ozzo organization in mid-2026, FURSY was already running in our internal services.

The Generic Methods Story

Before Go 1.27, if you wanted type-safe handlers in Go, your options were ugly:

// Package-level functions -- verbose, no type inference
fursy.POST[CreateUserReq, UserRes](router, "/users", handler)

// Or abandon type safety -- manual binding, no compile-time guarantees
router.Handle("POST", "/users", func(c *Context) error {
    var req CreateUserReq
    // manual JSON decode, manual validation, manual error handling...
})

Go 1.27 allows methods on concrete types to declare their own type parameters. This changes everything:

router.POST("/users", func(c *fursy.Box[CreateUserReq, UserRes]) error {
    // c.ReqBody is *CreateUserReq -- already validated, already bound
    user := createUser(c.ReqBody)
    return c.Created("/users/"+user.ID, UserRes{ID: user.ID, Name: user.Name})
})

No explicit type parameters at the call site. The compiler infers [CreateUserReq, UserRes] from the handler signature. Binding happens automatically before your handler runs -- if the JSON is malformed, the client gets a 400 before your code executes.

This sounds minor until you have 200 endpoints. The reduction in ceremony is significant.

What the Audit Found: CORS Was Echoing Everything

The most dangerous finding was in the CORS middleware. When a browser sends a preflight OPTIONS request, it includes Access-Control-Request-Headers listing which headers the JavaScript wants to use. The server should respond with only the headers it actually allows.

Our code:

// cors.go -- BEFORE the fix
func (cfg *CORSConfig) setPreflightHeaders(origin, method, reqHeaders string, headers http.Header) {
    allowed, allowedHeaders := cfg.isPreflightAllowed(origin, method, reqHeaders)
    if !allowed {
        return
    }
    // ...
    if allowedHeaders != "" {
        headers.Set("Access-Control-Allow-Headers", reqHeaders)  // BUG
    }
}

See it? isPreflightAllowed returns allowedHeaders (the filtered list), but line 225 writes reqHeaders (the raw request value). The browser sends Content-Type, X-Evil-Header, we configured the server to only allow Content-Type, and the response says "sure, X-Evil-Header is fine too."

The fix was one word:

headers.Set("Access-Control-Allow-Headers", allowedHeaders)  // FIXED

One word. Ninety-four percent test coverage didn't catch it because every test requested only headers that were in the allowlist. The regression test we added:

func TestCORS_PreflightFilteredHeaders(t *testing.T) {
    r := fursy.New()
    r.Use(CORSWithConfig(CORSConfig{
        AllowOrigins: "https://example.com",
        AllowMethods: "GET,POST",
        AllowHeaders: "Content-Type,Authorization",
    }))
    // ... setup ...

    req := httptest.NewRequest("OPTIONS", "/api", http.NoBody)
    req.Header.Set("Access-Control-Request-Headers", "Content-Type, X-Evil-Header")
    // ...

    got := w.Header().Get("Access-Control-Allow-Headers")
    if strings.Contains(got, "X-Evil-Header") {
        t.Errorf("preflight echoed disallowed header: got %q", got)
    }
}

Lesson: test the negative case. Every CORS test we had sent only valid headers.

The Documentation Was Lying

The auditor checked whether our docs matched the actual API. They didn't.

Document said Reality
router.Run(":8080") Method doesn't exist. Never did.
fursy.CSRF(fursy.CSRFConfig{...}) No CSRF middleware
fursy.Timeout(30 * time.Second) Doesn't exist
fursy.BodyLimit(10 * 1024 * 1024) Doesn't exist. Body limit is router.SetMaxBodySize()
fursy.HTTPSRedirect() Doesn't exist
fursy.RateLimit(100, time.Minute) Actual signature: middleware.RateLimit(float64, int). This wouldn't even compile.
import "encoding/json/v2" Code uses encoding/json. Go 1.27 made v2 the default behind this import.
SECURITY.md: supported versions 0.1.x, 0.2.x Current version: 0.5.4

Six non-existent APIs documented as if they were real. An LLM coding assistant reading our llms.md would confidently generate code that doesn't compile. A developer copying from SECURITY.md would get build errors.

How did this happen? The docs were written during the design phase and never reconciled with what was actually implemented. Classic drift -- the code evolves, the prose doesn't.

We cleaned out the worst offenders. Full documentation parity is still in progress -- doc drift is a hydra, and every time we grep for one stale reference, two more surface. The rule going forward: if the API doesn't exist in the source tree, it doesn't exist in the docs.

RFC 9457: Claiming It vs. Being It

Fursy's README said "Native RFC 9457 Problem Details." The auditor checked what GET /nonexistent actually returned:

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

Not Found

Plain text. Not JSON. Not RFC 9457. The "native" Problem Details only activated when a handler explicitly returned a fursy.Problem. Every auto-generated error -- 404, 405, 413, 415, 400, 500, and all middleware rejections -- was text/plain.

We fixed this across all paths:

// BEFORE -- text/plain
terminalHandler = func(ctx *Context) error {
    return ctx.String(http.StatusNotFound, "Not Found")
}

// AFTER -- RFC 9457
terminalHandler = func(ctx *Context) error {
    return ctx.Problem(NewProblem(http.StatusNotFound, "Not Found", ""))
}

Same change in JWT (401), BasicAuth (401), RateLimit (429), CircuitBreaker (503), Recovery (500). Every error response is now:

{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Not Found",
  "status": 404
}

With Content-Type: application/problem+json. This is a breaking change -- clients parsing text/plain error bodies will break. We shipped it in v0.6.0 because the project is pre-1.0 and the previous behavior was a lie.

The Colon That Broke Google's API Convention

A developer migrating from ozzo-routing reported that route registration panics:

router.GET("/clients:getOrganization/:id", handler1)
router.GET("/clients:getAddress/:id", handler2)
// panic: conflicting wildcard names: getOrganization vs getAddress

The : in clients:getOrganization was being parsed as a wildcard param marker. But this is a Google AIP-136 custom method -- the most widely adopted enterprise REST convention for non-CRUD operations. Google Firestore alone has 20+ endpoints using this pattern: /documents:commit, /documents:batchGet, /documents:rollback.

RFC 3986 Section 3.3 lists : as a legal path character. It doesn't need escaping. The :param convention is a Sinatra invention from 2007, not an RFC.

The fix: colons are wildcards only at segment start (after / or position 0):

// BEFORE
func findWildcardIndex(path string) int {
    for i := 0; i < len(path); i++ {
        if path[i] == ':' || path[i] == '*' {
            return i  // any position
        }
    }
    return -1
}

// AFTER
func findWildcardIndex(path string) int {
    for i := 0; i < len(path); i++ {
        if (path[i] == ':' || path[i] == '*') && (i == 0 || path[i-1] == '/') {
            return i  // segment start only
        }
    }
    return -1
}

For context: Gin fixed this in v1.11.0 after six years of open issues. Echo needed three separate PRs. httprouter never fixed it. Express.js has had it open since 2019.

Form Binding Errors: 500 Instead of 400

Submitting age=abc where age is an int field returned 500 Internal Server Error. The strconv parse error wasn't wrapped in our DecodeError type, so the error handler fell through to the catch-all:

// BEFORE -- raw error, caught by nothing
if err := setField(field, values[0]); err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("set field %s error: %w", structField.Name, err)
}

// AFTER -- wrapped, caught as 400
if err := setField(field, values[0]); err != nil {
    return &DecodeError{Err: fmt.Errorf("field %s: %w", structField.Name, err)}
}

A user sending ?age=abc now gets 400 Bad Request with a Problem Details body explaining which field failed. Not a 500 that makes your monitoring think the server is crashing.

This fix covers setField type mismatches. Errors from ParseForm/ParseMultipartForm itself (malformed percent-encoding, corrupt multipart boundaries) were also wrapped in v0.6.2.

What Fursy Doesn't Do

  • No ORM -- use Relica or GORM or raw database/sql
  • No migrations -- use goose or atlas
  • No template rendering -- this is an API router, not a web framework
  • No WebSocket/SSE built-in -- SSE works via the stream plugin; WebSocket upgrade requires the base responseWriter (no middleware wrappers in the chain) until stream adopts http.NewResponseController
  • No process management -- use daemon if you need it
  • No CSRF middleware -- we removed the docs that claimed it existed. If you need CSRF, use gorilla/csrf or write your own. We'll add it when we have a design we're confident in, not before.

Fursy vs. Other Go Routers (2026)

Router Go Version Type Safety Allocs/op Error Format Colon Literal Dependencies
Go 1.22+ stdlib 1.22+ {param} only ~3 text/plain Yes ({param}) 0
chi v5 1.22+ {param} only ~2 text/plain Yes ({param}) 0
Gin 1.18+ No generics 0 custom JSON Yes (v1.11+) 8
Echo 1.18+ No generics 1 custom JSON Yes (escaped) 4
Fiber 1.21+ No generics 0 text/plain No fasthttp
fursy 1.27+ Generic methods 0 (plain) / 2 (generic) RFC 9457 Yes (v0.6.2) 2 (JWT, rate)

Fursy requires Go 1.27. That's a hard requirement. If you're on 1.22 or earlier, use chi or the stdlib mux. If you want zero dependencies, use the stdlib. If you need the fastest raw throughput, Fiber on fasthttp wins.

Fursy is for teams that want type-safe handlers, zero-alloc routing, and RFC-compliant error responses in a single package, and can target Go 1.27+.

Numbers

Metric Value
Core library ~8,200 lines
Test code ~16,000 lines (2:1 ratio)
Test functions 510+ (core + plugins)
Benchmarks 21
Coverage 93.8% core, 96.5% middleware
Static route lookup <100 ns/op, 0 alloc
Parametric route lookup <140 ns/op, 0 alloc
Production dependencies 2 (golang-jwt, x/time)
Plugin dependencies Isolated per plugin
CI checks 12 (3 OS, lint, format, vuln, 4 plugins, examples, codecov)
External audit findings 45 claims checked, 33 confirmed, all fixed in v0.6.0-v0.6.2

Gotchas

router.GET Is a Generic Method Now

After v0.5.0, router.GET expects Handler[Req, Res] (a function taking *Box[Req, Res]), not HandlerFunc (taking *Context). For plain handlers without type-safe binding:

// This does NOT compile:
router.GET("/health", func(c *fursy.Context) error { ... })

// Use Handle for plain handlers:
router.Handle("GET", "/health", func(c *fursy.Context) error { ... })

// Or use the generic form with Empty types:
router.GET("/health", func(c *fursy.Box[fursy.Empty, fursy.Empty]) error { ... })

Plugins Have Their Own go.mod

Each plugin (plugins/opentelemetry, plugins/database, plugins/stream, plugins/validator) is a separate Go module. When upgrading fursy, update the plugin's go.mod too:

cd plugins/stream
go get github.com/coregx/fursy@v0.6.2
go mod tidy

CORS Must Be Global

CORS middleware must be registered at the router level (router.Use()), not on a group. Preflight OPTIONS requests hit the global middleware chain before route matching. Group-level CORS will miss them. This matches Gin, Echo, and Chi behavior.

The Second Pass

The first audit found the CORS echo, the phantom docs, and the text/plain lie. We fixed those in v0.6.0. Then we sent the fix branch back for re-validation. The second pass found 11 more: an open redirect in the trailing-slash handler, WebSocket hijack broken by our own response wrapper, the circuit breaker counting 404s as backend failures, and the OpenAPI generator not knowing about the colon fix it shipped alongside. All fixed in v0.6.2.

The pattern is humbling: every fix creates a surface for the next bug. The CORS allowlist fix shipped next to a default that had been blocking JSON POST preflights all along -- no test ever sent one. The colon fix in the radix tree didn't propagate to the OpenAPI converter. The response wrapper that tracked written didn't implement Hijack. Ninety-four percent coverage catches syntax, not semantics.

Try It 

go get github.com/coregx/fursy@v0.6.2

The project is at v0.6.2. The API is not frozen -- we're pre-1.0 and will break things when the design demands it. The llms.md documents every API pattern for both developers and AI coding assistants.

coregx/fursy -- Type-safe HTTP router for Go 1.27+. RFC 9457 errors. Zero-alloc routing. MIT license.

title: Logistics Hiring Scores Using Unified Node Backend Proxy with One API Key and Retries
description:
Short answer: a Node backend proxy should expose one API key and one unified endpoint while OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, and Google Gemini credentials remain behind the server boundary. Internal model aliases are mapped there, and only transient failures are retried. For logistics candidate scoring, the deciding outcome is valid, rubric-bound JSON. Provider breadth comes second.

Choice Client credential Structured-output control Operating burden Best fit
Direct provider SDKs One per provider Provider-specific Low at first Experiments tied to one provider
Managed multi-provider gateway One gateway key Common envelope, with provider differences still visible Low to medium A solo team that needs several providers now
Self-hosted routing proxy One internal key Fully owned normalization and validation High Strict network or policy control

Recommendation: for a one-person SaaS shipping weekly, start with a managed gateway only if it preserves structured responses and exposes retry metadata. Otherwise, put a thin internal adapter in front of direct SDKs. Do not build a general-purpose router. Outsource the undifferentiated transport work, but own the hiring rubric, schema, validation, and audit record.

A single key is a client-facing abstraction, not a universal provider credential. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google each document their own authentication and request surfaces. Your browser or mobile client should never receive those upstream secrets. The backend holds them, while callers authenticate to one endpoint with one application-scoped secret.

How should a Node backend proxy use one API key?

The first criterion is schema fidelity. A candidate-scoring response that looks plausible but swaps a score for a string is not a partial success. It is rejected data. The same goes for a response that invents a rubric category, omits evidence, or returns a score outside the allowed range. The proxy should authenticate the caller, resolve the alias, send the provider-specific request, normalize the result, and validate the final object before returning it. That is the whole useful path; adding provider discovery, prompt catalogs, or a generic workflow engine would enlarge the maintenance surface without improving this decision.

Invalid means invalid.

Use JSON Schema as the contract. Draft 2020-12 defines validation vocabulary for object shape, required properties, numeric bounds, and whether extra properties are permitted. Provider-native structured-output features can help produce the shape, but the application must still validate the received value. Providers document different structured-output mechanisms and supported schema subsets, so a unified envelope must not pretend their behavior is identical.

For this job, I would measure four outcomes per internal alias: valid JSON, schema-valid JSON, rubric-valid content, and terminal failure. Keep them separate. A parser error and an unsupported extra field lead to different fixes. So does a valid object whose evidence is absent from the supplied resume.

The second criterion is failure semantics. Retry only failures that may succeed without changing the request: rate limits, transient server failures, and transport interruption. Do not retry an authentication failure. Do not blindly retry invalid output either; repeated sampling can multiply cost and latency without correcting a bad contract. One constrained repair attempt can be reasonable when the response is parseable and the validation errors are explicit, but record it as a repair, not a first-pass success.

This is where the revenue-per-hour lens helps. A broad abstraction is expensive to maintain. A narrow port with five observable outcomes is boring, and boring leaves time to ship the feature customers use. The explicit trade-off is less freedom for each call site in exchange for one enforceable contract.

The smallest useful contract

Keep provider model identifiers out of product code. The application asks for a capability alias such as rubric-strict; deployment configuration maps that alias to a concrete upstream model. Changing the map then becomes an evaluated release, not a search-and-replace operation.

import { z } from "zod";

const CandidateScore = z.object({
  candidateId: z.string().min(1),
  recommendation: z.enum(["advance", "review", "decline"]),
  criteria: z.array(
    z.object({
      rubricId: z.string().min(1),
      score: z.number().int().min(0).max(4),
      evidence: z.array(z.string().min(1)).max(3),
    }).strict(),
  ).min(1),
}).strict();

type CandidateScore = z.infer<typeof CandidateScore>;

type GenerateRequest = {
  model: "rubric-strict" | "rubric-fast";
  input: { candidateId: string; resumeText: string; rubric: string };
  idempotencyKey: string;
};

type GenerateResult = {
  value: CandidateScore;
  providerRequestId?: string;
  attempts: number;
};

interface ModelGateway {
  generate(request: GenerateRequest): Promise<GenerateResult>;
}

export async function scoreCandidate(
  gateway: ModelGateway,
  request: GenerateRequest,
): Promise<GenerateResult> {
  const result = await gateway.generate(request);
  return { ...result, value: CandidateScore.parse(result.value) };
}

The schema is intentionally tight: scores are integers from 0 through 4, recommendations are enumerated, and unknown keys fail validation. Those numbers describe this example rubric, not a benchmark or a universal hiring standard. The evidence strings should quote or point to material already present in the candidate input; a later deterministic check can verify that grounding rule.

Keep environment configuration equally small. Parse it once during startup and fail before accepting traffic.

import { z } from "zod";

const Env = z.object({
  MODEL_GATEWAY_URL: z.string().url(),
  MODEL_GATEWAY_KEY: z.string().min(1),
  MODEL_RUBRIC_STRICT: z.string().min(1),
  MODEL_RUBRIC_FAST: z.string().min(1),
});

export const env = Env.parse(process.env);

export const modelMap = {
  "rubric-strict": env.MODEL_RUBRIC_STRICT,
  "rubric-fast": env.MODEL_RUBRIC_FAST,
} as const;

Use a secret manager in production and inject values at runtime. Do not commit an .env file. Rotate the gateway key independently from upstream keys, and scope it to the service that needs it. One leaked application key should not reveal three upstream credentials.

Keep secrets dull.

How should retries preserve correctness?

Set one end-to-end deadline. Then fit attempts inside it. If an HTTP call has already consumed most of the request budget, another attempt is not resilience; it is a late response waiting to happen.

Exponential backoff with jitter reduces synchronized retries. Honor Retry-After when the upstream sends it, cap the number of attempts, and attach an idempotency key when the gateway supports one. The caller should see a stable error category such as rate_limited, upstream_unavailable, invalid_output, or unauthorized, while logs retain the upstream status and request identifier.

Streaming needs a separate decision. Server-Sent Events use the text/event-stream media type and reconnect by default in browsers. That is useful for generated prose. It is awkward for a score object that must be validated as a whole. For hiring scores, buffer the structured response, validate it, and only then return JSON. Correct first.

Do not log resumes, prompts, raw credentials, or complete model responses by default. Log the internal alias, resolved model version or identifier, schema version, latency, attempt count, validation outcome, token usage when supplied, and request IDs. Candidate material is sensitive operational data even when the article's main concern is model routing.

An evaluation set should include ordinary resumes plus adversarial cases: an empty employment section, conflicting dates, instructions embedded in resume text, missing rubric categories, and Unicode-heavy input. Run it before changing an alias. Compare first-pass schema validity and rubric assertions, not a single aggregate quality score. Ten hand-picked happy paths can catch wiring errors; they cannot establish production quality.

When is the runner-up the better choice?

Direct SDKs are the better runner-up when only one provider is in production, structured output is the dominant requirement, and its native feature exposes controls your common gateway cannot represent. OpenAI documents Structured Outputs with JSON Schema, Anthropic documents tool definitions built around input schemas, and Google documents schema-controlled JSON output. These are related mechanisms, not interchangeable contracts. Keeping a small provider adapter can preserve their useful differences.

Self-hosting wins when policy requires traffic to remain inside a controlled network, when custom admission rules must execute before every request, or when gateway observability is insufficient for an audit. Accept the trade: patching, capacity, secret rotation, telemetry, and on-call ownership now belong to you. For a solo SaaS, that work competes directly with the weekly release.

A managed gateway is attractive when multiple providers are already necessary and its normalized response retains the fields you need. Its limitation is the extra network hop and the possibility that normalization hides a provider-specific structured-output control. It is not appropriate when either issue breaks the scoring contract; use a direct adapter instead. Verify cancellation, timeout propagation, retry behavior, structured-output support, and access to provider request IDs before adopting it. A demo that returns text proves very little about a logistics scoring pipeline.

The durable boundary is small: one client credential, capability aliases, a versioned schema, explicit failure categories, and an evaluation gate. Everything behind it may change. The rubric and the acceptance test should not.

References

  • https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/json-schema-core
  • https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/json-schema-validation
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events/Using_server-sent_events
  • https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/structured-outputs
  • https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/tool-use
  • https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/structured-output
  • https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#name-retry-after

title: Processing ISO 20022 payment XML in Rust: detection, typed parsing and JSON
description:
ISO 20022 payment messages are versioned XML documents. In an integration service, the first task may be to identify a message and read a few business fields. A later stage may need typed field access, arithmetic on an amount, and serialization for another system.

This walkthrough uses rust_iso20022 0.1.6, an Apache-2.0 toolkit with a Rust 1.85 core MSRV. Its generated model collection covers 1,130 message versions across 32 business areas, including earlier versions. We'll use just one message version, pacs.008.001.08.

The XML below is a synthetic, intentionally minimal teaching sample. It demonstrates the SDK's parsing APIs; it is not a complete schema-valid or scheme-approved payment instruction. None of the examples performs complete XSD or banking-scheme validation.

Start with the model-free core. Create a Rust application and add the published version:

cargo new iso20022-demo
cd iso20022-demo
cargo add rust_iso20022@0.1.6

Replace src/main.rs with this complete program:

use rust_iso20022::{detect, MxNode};

const XML: &str = r#"<Document xmlns="urn:iso:std:iso:20022:tech:xsd:pacs.008.001.08">
  <FIToFICstmrCdtTrf>
    <GrpHdr><MsgId>DEMO-001</MsgId><NbOfTxs>1</NbOfTxs></GrpHdr>
    <CdtTrfTxInf>
      <PmtId><EndToEndId>E2E-DEMO-001</EndToEndId></PmtId>
      <IntrBkSttlmAmt Ccy="EUR">1234.56</IntrBkSttlmAmt>
    </CdtTrfTxInf>
  </FIToFICstmrCdtTrf>
</Document>"#;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let id = detect(XML).ok_or("unrecognized ISO 20022 message")?;
    println!("message: {}", id.message_name());

    let tree = MxNode::parse(XML).ok_or("invalid XML")?;
    let message_id = tree.find("MsgId").and_then(|node| node.text());
    println!("message_id: {}", message_id.unwrap_or(""));

    let amount = tree.find("IntrBkSttlmAmt").ok_or("missing amount")?;
    println!(
        "amount: {} {}",
        amount.text().unwrap_or(""),
        amount.attr("Ccy").unwrap_or("")
    );
    Ok(())
}

Run it:

cargo run

For this sample, the output is:

message: pacs.008.001.08
message_id: DEMO-001
amount: 1234.56 EUR

detect reads the message identity from its XML namespace. MxNode provides generic tree access, so no generated payment types are required. The example has one amount and one group header. In multi-transaction or enveloped messages, navigate the relevant subtree or use the business-message helpers; a generic first-match field lookup is not a complete payment routing policy.

Now add typed parsing, JSON and decimal conversion:

cargo add rust_iso20022@0.1.6 --features model-pacs,serde,convert

model-pacs compiles the pacs family, serde enables JSON serialization and convert provides decimal/date helpers. Replace src/main.rs with the following complete program:

use rust_iso20022::generated::pacs::pacs_008_001_08::Document;
use rust_iso20022::{detect, from_xml, to_json, to_xml};

const XML: &str = r#"<Document xmlns="urn:iso:std:iso:20022:tech:xsd:pacs.008.001.08">
  <FIToFICstmrCdtTrf>
    <GrpHdr><MsgId>DEMO-001</MsgId><NbOfTxs>1</NbOfTxs></GrpHdr>
    <CdtTrfTxInf>
      <PmtId><EndToEndId>E2E-DEMO-001</EndToEndId></PmtId>
      <IntrBkSttlmAmt Ccy="EUR">1234.56</IntrBkSttlmAmt>
    </CdtTrfTxInf>
  </FIToFICstmrCdtTrf>
</Document>"#;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let id = detect(XML).ok_or("unrecognized ISO 20022 message")?;
    println!("message: {}", id.message_name());

    let document: Document = from_xml(XML)?;
    let payment = &document.fi_to_fi_cstmr_cdt_trf;
    println!("message_id: {}", payment.grp_hdr.msg_id.0);

    let amount = &payment.cdt_trf_tx_inf[0].intr_bk_sttlm_amt;
    println!("amount: {} {}", amount.value, amount.ccy.0);

    let decimal = rust_iso20022::convert::to_decimal(&amount.value)
        .ok_or("invalid decimal amount")?;
    println!("doubled: {}", decimal + decimal);

    let serialized_xml = to_xml(&document)?;
    let reparsed: Document = from_xml(&serialized_xml)?;
    println!("xml_round_trip: {}", document == reparsed);

    println!("json: {}", to_json(&document)?);
    Ok(())
}

Run cargo run again. The lines before the JSON document are:

message: pacs.008.001.08
message_id: DEMO-001
amount: 1234.56 EUR
doubled: 2469.12
xml_round_trip: true

The field path refers directly to the generated Document. Financial scalars retain their string representation; the conversion helper returns a Decimal for arithmetic without introducing a binary floating-point amount. The equality check demonstrates an XML round-trip for this sample and these SDK types. It does not imply preservation of the original whitespace, prefix spelling or byte sequence.

The final line serializes the generated model to JSON for internal application processing. JSON output is not a claim that a banking network accepts JSON in place of its required ISO 20022 XML format.

The default feature set is empty. For typed processing, choose the needed business family rather than enabling the aggregate model feature. Compiling all 1,130 models together has substantial compilation and memory cost; even the pacs family adds more build work than the inspection core.

Validation is a separate decision. Complete offline XSD validation is not implemented. Generated-message L2 binding currently covers pacs.008.001.08, and CBPR+/SEPA public-reference checks are provisional developer checks rather than complete production rule packs or bank certification. Parsing or round-tripping this sample does not establish scheme compliance.

For a larger integration flow and existing examples:

  • Payment pipeline example
  • Feature selection
  • Coverage and limitations
  • API documentation
  • Repository and crates.io package

If you process ISO 20022 in Rust, which message versions and field-access workflows would make the most useful next examples?

Disclosure: This tutorial was prepared with AI assistance. The code examples were compiled and run locally against SDK source corresponding to the 0.1.6 release.
